report:
**Conclusion:** Ginkgo biloba extract is **not a proven treatment for tinnitus**. The best current systematic review (12 randomized trials; 1,915 participants) found the evidence too uncertain/low quality to show a meaningful benefit over placebo; studies had important bias and reporting limitations. Thus, it should not be expected to reliably reduce tinnitus loudness or distress. [https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013514_ginkgo-biloba-herbal-supplement-tinnitus](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013514_ginkgo-biloba-herbal-supplement-tinnitus)

This aligns with the U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, which says research does not support ginkgo for relieving tinnitus symptoms. [https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginkgo](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginkgo)

Clinical guidance likewise advises clinicians **not** to recommend ginkgo or other dietary supplements for persistent, bothersome tinnitus. [https://www.ata.org/about-tinnitus/is-there-a-magic-pill/](https://www.ata.org/about-tinnitus/is-there-a-magic-pill/)

If tinnitus is new, one-sided, pulsating, accompanies sudden hearing loss, dizziness, or neurologic symptoms, seek prompt medical evaluation. Otherwise, discuss evidence-based management (hearing assessment, sound strategies, and tinnitus-focused cognitive behavioral therapy) with a clinician rather than relying on ginkgo.
